item.dc:creator: Mike Wall
item.content:encoded: null NASA's Swift space telescope has reached the end of its long and winding road. Swift fell uncontrolled to Earth today (Nov. 4), 22 years after it launched but just three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost it to a higher, life-extending orbit. The 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) today over northern Sumatra, according to satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell , who cited U.S. Space Force data. The fall likely didn't make much of an impact; NASA officials predicted beforehand that most of the minibus-sized Swift would burn up as it fell, and they put the odds of any of the surviving pieces hurting anyone on Earth at just 1 in 2,100. Swift — officially known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer — launched to Earth orbit in November 2004 on a two-year mission to study gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most powerful explosions in the universe . "Swift" was not an acronym but rather referred to the spacecraft's observational agility. "Swift needed to detect and locate gamma-ray bursts, communicate their position to other observatories, and then swing its telescopes around to image the burst locations before their afterglows faded out," S. Bradley Cenko, Swift's principal investigator (PI) at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, said in an Oct. 23 statement . "This typically took Swift about a minute to do." Swift didn't just observe GRBs. It also studied a variety of other cosmic bodies and phenomena, from faraway supernova explosions and feeding black holes to asteroids and comets in our own solar system. And it kept doing this long after its warranty expired — for about 20 years after, in fact. The space telescope didn't conduct its final science observation until this past Oct. 20 . (Swift underwent a name change during this stretch: In 2018, it was rechristened the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory after its first PI, who died the previous year.) "Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long," Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA's Astrophysics Division, said in the same Oct. 23 statement. "In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community," he added. Katalyst Space’s LINK robotic servicing spacecraft captured this view of one of its solar panels in Earth orbit in August 2026. (Image credit: Katalyst Space)) Swift was incredibly productive, observing more than 2,000 GRBs and 1,400 supernovas over the course of its long scientific life. But it could have gathered even more data, had a dramatic rescue mission worked out. In September 2025, NASA awarded the Arizona company Katalyst Space a $30 million contract to design, launch and operate a robotic spacecraft that would meet up with Swift and boost it to a higher orbit, thus extending its operational life. Swift was falling back to Earth: It had no onboard thrusters to counteract the effect of atmospheric drag, which had been pulling the observatory down ever since it launched. The process was accelerating as Swift got lower, so Katalyst had to work fast. And the company did: It launched its refrigerator-sized, three-armed LINK servicing spacecraft on July 3 , targeting an August capture of Swift. That didn't happen, however. LINK suffered problems with its propulsion system and orientation-maintaining reaction wheels, which nixed the planned meetup. Still, it was a worthwhile effort, according to NASA. "From the beginning, this was a high-risk, high-reward mission," Domagal-Goldman said in a statement on Sept. 25 , the day that LINK itself crashed back to Earth. "And while we'll be sad to see Swift's mission come to a close, we knew this boost effort would be worthwhile either way — advancing U.S. spacecraft servicing technology, challenging us to meet unprecedented mission timelines, and testing how we operate satellites to extend their time in low Earth orbit ," he added. Swift's crash today wasn't exactly unusual, by the way. At least three large objects — dead satellites or spent rocket bodies — fall back to Earth every day on average, a 2025 report found . And that number is bound to rise in the coming years, as humanity builds out more and more megaconstellations in Earth orbit.

item.title: Trump says impeaching him would ‘destroy’ Democrats
item.description: US President Donald Trump said Wednesday that if the Democrats were to launch an effort to impeach him when they take control of Congress next year, it would “destroy” their party. Asked about prospective impeachment a day after his Republican Party suffered a sweeping midterm election loss, Trump said: “I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that,” insisting there was “no reason” for him to be impeached. item.title: Billions in revenue proves Fifa right on the World Cup – but only on things it cares about
item.description: The 2026 edition of the tournament brought in untold amounts of money to Gianni Infantino’s governing body The total hasn’t entirely stopped rising yet, still clicking away towards a final tally. Still, Fifa has already announced that it surpassed its own lofty revenue projections for the 2026 World Cup, bringing in $15bn, significantly more than anticipated. It appears that a third of that total – $5bn – came from ticket sales and hospitality alone, per reporting from the Times . That would mean direct income from the matchgoing fans came in five times as high in the United States, Canada and Mexico as it did at the last World Cup, in Qatar in 2022, when the total stood at $929m. While 2026’s expanded World Cup added 40 games to the schedule, the takings nevertheless went from an average of about $14.5m per match to about $48m. Continue reading...

item.title: Brandon Sanderson’s Mistborn TTRPG Lays the Groundwork for His Next Series
item.description: Last year, Brotherwise Games published a set of three tabletop role-playing game books set in the world of Brandon Sanderson’s epic fantasy series The Stormlight Archive . The company quickly followed up the project by announcing an expansion to the Cosmere RPG based on Sanderson’s Mistborn setting, and the new books reveal the true scope of the company’s ambitions.

item.title: Toothbrush that emits electricity may more effectively prevent gum disease
item.description: A new and improved toothbrush could help avoid trips to the dentist Westend61/Alamy A toothbrush that generates electricity may more effectively fight harmful bacteria, while removing plaque, than existing products. The toothbrush uses special bristles that produce electricity as they bend, triggering the formation of molecules that damage bacterial membranes. When put to the test, it led to more than twice the reduction of plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding as conventional toothbrushes. “The concept is great,” says Nicholas Jakubovics at Newcastle University, UK, who wasn’t involved in the research. “Basically, the mechanical forces recharge the surface, so it’s really innovative. Anything that even slightly improves the way dental care works could have a benefit, because oral disease is just so widespread.” Read more How regrowing your own teeth could replace dentures and implants Oral diseases, such as tooth decay, affect nearly half the global population . Brushing regularly can help remove plaque, a sticky layer of bacteria that forms on teeth. These bacteria can produce acids that cause cavities and irritate gums, sometimes leading to tooth loss. Advertisement But even thorough brushing can leave behind bacteria deep in plaque or between teeth, allowing colonies to grow back within hours. Researchers have previously developed toothbrushes with antibacterial metal nanoparticles, including silver and zinc, embedded in their bristles , although their long-term effectiveness is uncertain. Others have designed ionic toothbrushes that use electric currents to help loosen plaque , but they are dependent on batteries. Now, Yanhui Lu at Peking University in China and her colleagues have turned to studies showing that so-called piezoelectric materials fight bacteria in infected wounds and medical implants. These generate electric charges under pressure , prompting Lu’s team to develop toothbrush bristles made from piezoelectric plastic. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter The idea was that, as the bristles bend during brushing, they would generate electricity, triggering chemical reactions that produce molecules called reactive-oxygen species that damage bacteria, while the bristles physically remove plaque. The researchers made two sets of bristles of different thicknesses, both of which met Chinese national standards for softness and strength. Laboratory tests confirmed the bristles generated electricity under pressure, particularly the thicker ones. The team also detected reactive-oxygen species on the brushes, which remained soft and retained their electrical properties after three months of use. Next, the researchers exposed two common oral bacteria to their bristles and nylon ones, which are used in standard toothbrushes, in laboratory experiments, including simulated brushing movements. item.content:encoded: A new and improved toothbrush could help avoid trips to the dentist Westend61/Alamy A toothbrush that generates electricity may more effectively fight harmful bacteria, while removing plaque, than existing products. The toothbrush uses special bristles that produce electricity as they bend, triggering the formation of molecules that damage bacterial membranes. When put to the test, it led to more than twice the reduction of plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding as conventional toothbrushes. “The concept is great,” says Nicholas Jakubovics at Newcastle University, UK, who wasn’t involved in the research. “Basically, the mechanical forces recharge the surface, so it’s really innovative. Anything that even slightly improves the way dental care works could have a benefit, because oral disease is just so widespread.” Read more How regrowing your own teeth could replace dentures and implants Oral diseases, such as tooth decay, affect nearly half the global population . Brushing regularly can help remove plaque, a sticky layer of bacteria that forms on teeth. These bacteria can produce acids that cause cavities and irritate gums, sometimes leading to tooth loss. Advertisement But even thorough brushing can leave behind bacteria deep in plaque or between teeth, allowing colonies to grow back within hours. Researchers have previously developed toothbrushes with antibacterial metal nanoparticles, including silver and zinc, embedded in their bristles , although their long-term effectiveness is uncertain. Others have designed ionic toothbrushes that use electric currents to help loosen plaque , but they are dependent on batteries. Now, Yanhui Lu at Peking University in China and her colleagues have turned to studies showing that so-called piezoelectric materials fight bacteria in infected wounds and medical implants. These generate electric charges under pressure , prompting Lu’s team to develop toothbrush bristles made from piezoelectric plastic. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter The idea was that, as the bristles bend during brushing, they would generate electricity, triggering chemical reactions that produce molecules called reactive-oxygen species that damage bacteria, while the bristles physically remove plaque. The researchers made two sets of bristles of different thicknesses, both of which met Chinese national standards for softness and strength. Laboratory tests confirmed the bristles generated electricity under pressure, particularly the thicker ones. The team also detected reactive-oxygen species on the brushes, which remained soft and retained their electrical properties after three months of use. Next, the researchers exposed two common oral bacteria to their bristles and nylon ones, which are used in standard toothbrushes, in laboratory experiments, including simulated brushing movements. The thicker piezoelectric bristles were particularly effective, killing about 53 per cent of Streptococcus mutans , which causes cavities, and 78 per cent of Porphyromonas gingivalis , which contributes to gum disease, compared with just 9 and 8 per cent, respectively, for nylon bristles. The team also grew plaque from human mouths on pieces of cow enamel and brushed them for 3 minutes. The new toothbrushes removed more than 99 per cent of the plaque, compared with about 80 per cent for conventional nylon brushes. Finally, the team tested the toothbrushes in 109 adults with dental plaque and gum inflammation, who were randomly assigned to use either a piezoelectric or nylon toothbrush twice daily for three months. Dental examinations revealed reductions of roughly 40 per cent in plaque build-up, gum inflammation and bleeding among those using the piezoelectric brushes, compared with around 15 per cent for those using conventional brushes. Genetic sequencing of the dental plaque from the piezoelectric group also revealed a decline in the relative abundance of harmful bacteria and an increase in some potentially beneficial bacteria. Larger studies now need to establish whether the toothbrush actually prevents issues like cavities and tooth loss, says Jakubovics. Journal Reference: Science Advances DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg5744

item.title: Mars isn't dead — recent volcanic activity reveals it's just sleeping
item.description: null Scientists have long suspected that Mars is geologically "dead," but new spacecraft observations suggest the Red Planet's volcanoes are merely sleeping. That means that Olympus Mons , the extinct Martian volcano that at around 16 miles (26 kilometers) above the surrounding Martian plains is the largest mountain in the solar system , may in fact be a slumbering giant. The observations were made with the European Space Agency (ESA) mission ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) as it studied volcanic fissures along the Alba Mons region of the Red Planet. Alba Mons is in the Tharsis region of Mars, the same area that is home to Olympus Mons. While the latter is the tallest volcano in the solar system, at 374 miles (600 km) across, about the size of Arizona, the Alba Mons region is the largest volcano when considering surface area. TGO detected gas containing hydrogen chloride making its way to the surface of Mars through the Alba Mons fissures. The same gas is commonly found escaping from magmatic vents on Earth, with the compound coming from hot magma beneath the surface. Detecting it on Mars is a sign of dormant Martian volcanism. Orbital imagery had previously shown some volcanoes appear to have been active within the last few million years, and seismometers have detected the rumbling of "marsquakes," both implying the Red Planet is volcanically active. However, eruptions and lava flows have been conspicuous by their absence. "Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," team co-leader and scientist at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences, Daniel Mège, said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "The TGO was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack." Evidence of dormant Martian volcanism is rising Mège and colleagues were first alerted to something strange happening on Mars when they noticed spikes of hydrogen chloride during Martian summer and on the northern hemisphere of the Red Planet. That is both a time and place at which hydrogen chloride shouldn't be detected. The gas usually peaks in the northern hemisphere during winter on Mars, disappearing in the summer. This variation is connected to the water and dust cycle on Mars. An exception to the rule occurs over volcanic fissures on the flanks of the Alba Mons volcano, in early summer. The TGO followed up on this by detecting fresh and narrow fissures, in some cases hundreds of feet long, in the Alba Mons region. A clear sign of volcanism. "It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," Mège said. An animated gif of an Elongated Cloud over the Alba Mons. (Image credit: ESA/GCP/UVP/EHU Bilbao.) item.dc:creator: Robert Lea
item.content:encoded: null Scientists have long suspected that Mars is geologically "dead," but new spacecraft observations suggest the Red Planet's volcanoes are merely sleeping. That means that Olympus Mons , the extinct Martian volcano that at around 16 miles (26 kilometers) above the surrounding Martian plains is the largest mountain in the solar system , may in fact be a slumbering giant. The observations were made with the European Space Agency (ESA) mission ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) as it studied volcanic fissures along the Alba Mons region of the Red Planet. Alba Mons is in the Tharsis region of Mars, the same area that is home to Olympus Mons. While the latter is the tallest volcano in the solar system, at 374 miles (600 km) across, about the size of Arizona, the Alba Mons region is the largest volcano when considering surface area. TGO detected gas containing hydrogen chloride making its way to the surface of Mars through the Alba Mons fissures. The same gas is commonly found escaping from magmatic vents on Earth, with the compound coming from hot magma beneath the surface. Detecting it on Mars is a sign of dormant Martian volcanism. Orbital imagery had previously shown some volcanoes appear to have been active within the last few million years, and seismometers have detected the rumbling of "marsquakes," both implying the Red Planet is volcanically active. However, eruptions and lava flows have been conspicuous by their absence. "Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," team co-leader and scientist at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences, Daniel Mège, said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "The TGO was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack." Evidence of dormant Martian volcanism is rising Mège and colleagues were first alerted to something strange happening on Mars when they noticed spikes of hydrogen chloride during Martian summer and on the northern hemisphere of the Red Planet. That is both a time and place at which hydrogen chloride shouldn't be detected. The gas usually peaks in the northern hemisphere during winter on Mars, disappearing in the summer. This variation is connected to the water and dust cycle on Mars. An exception to the rule occurs over volcanic fissures on the flanks of the Alba Mons volcano, in early summer. The TGO followed up on this by detecting fresh and narrow fissures, in some cases hundreds of feet long, in the Alba Mons region. A clear sign of volcanism. "It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," Mège said. An animated gif of an Elongated Cloud over the Alba Mons. (Image credit: ESA/GCP/UVP/EHU Bilbao.) The team thinks that these gases have been rising from the interior of Mars during the Martian winter, becoming blocked by ice. When this ice sublimates, changes directly from solid to gas, during summer, the gas is released, prompting spikes in hydrogen chloride seen by the TGO. "Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated," said Mège. "A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere. "We needed to be rigorous, critical and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food." Implications for life on Mars? Mège and colleagues theorize that the gas is connected to "volcanic plumbing" in the form of a dormant magma chamber under the surface of Mars. Regions like this could become hotspots (pun not intended) in the search for life on Mars . That is because magmatic gases like hydrogen chloride would have been more abundant in the past, creating a thicker Martian atmosphere and warmer climate. Not only would this have led to liquid water covering much of the Martian surface, but when lava bubbled through the Martian crust and met groundwater, warm habitable niches ideal for microbial life could have been forged. "Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface," Mège concluded. The team's research was published in the journal Science Advances on Wednesday (Nov. 4).

item.title: Xbox previews two new ways to control cloud games
item.description: I revealed yesterday that the new Xbox Nano controller supports a Wi-Fi connection directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming, and now Microsoft is making it official today. Two new Xbox previews will let players try out using a phone as a controller on smart TVs, as well as cloud connect on the Xbox Nano to connect directly to cloud servers. "Instead of a Bluetooth connection to your TV, cloud connect uses your Wi-Fi to connect directly to the cloud server running your game," says the Xbox team . "That can help reduce input latency, so gameplay may feel more responsive." Players in the US will be able to preview the new cloud connect option for the Xbo … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: Fedora 45 is finally finished and fit
item.description: Fedora 45 is here , after not one but two week-long delays as the team found last-minute issues. Although both the original and second announcements were irksomely non-specific, in general we prefer this "when it's ready" approach to the rigid calendar-based schedule that Canonical favors for Ubuntu. It includes six main editions, five immutable desktop variants, and 12 "spins" with different GUIs. The combined version 45 release notes detail some of the bigger individual component changes and note the hardware requirements. The recommended spec is now a 2 GHz quad-core CPU with 8 GB of RAM and 20 GB of disk space, and at least 1024×768 graphics. Fedora 45 supports most display adapters, but 3D acceleration may not work on older GPUs, including Intel models prior to GMA9xx, Nvidia models prior to NV30 (GeForce FX5xxx series), and AMD Radeon models prior to R300 (Radeon 9500). We took a quick look at the beta back in September, focusing on its new next-generation text console, which is a welcome change. We especially liked the ability to zoom in and out on the text console on the fly, which is something we've missed since the superb "Laptop Ultravision" for DOS , about a third of a century ago. (The company is long gone, but we found a downloadable version for all you DOS users .) The desktop flagship editions are Workstation 45 , which comes with GNOME 51 "A Coruña" , and Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop , with KDE Plasma 6.8 . We covered some of the new features in GNOME 51 when we looked at the Ubuntu 26.10 beta , and those changes apply here too – notably, improvements in the Settings app, but removal of some older Nvidia GPU support. Both the big names are Wayland-only environments now, but by our reckoning, X11 fans have seven of the 12 official spins to choose from: Xfce, Cinnamon, MATE, i3, LXQt, LXDE, and Sugar (SOAS) all still use X.org if you prefer. There is also a combined What's New page for all the Atomic Desktops, Fedora’s immutable variants – the main shared feature here being the new web-based installer. The new version of main Fedora is accompanied by Fedora Asahi Remix 45 for Apple Silicon Macs. This is a more notable release than the cross-platform editions, as Asahi 45 brings initial support for M3-based Macs as well as M1 and M2 kit. As The Reg described in September , though, the M3 support is preliminary and limited – for instance, it excludes the M3 Ultra. If you have an M3 Mac, for now, you're better off sticking to macOS. The most important changes in Fedora 45 are under the hood, which is what the Red Hat release announcement focuses on. It now uses RPM version 6.1, with enhanced package signature checking , and blocks the vendor of packages silently changing. The GNOME keyring now uses the oo7 secrets manager . Support for two old VPN plugins has been removed, because the packages were unmaintained. A feature that we are happy to see land at last is better support for Red Hat’s Stratis next-generation storage subsystem. We g
item.dc:creator: Liam Proven
item.content:encoded: Fedora 45 is here , after not one but two week-long delays as the team found last-minute issues. Although both the original and second announcements were irksomely non-specific, in general we prefer this "when it's ready" approach to the rigid calendar-based schedule that Canonical favors for Ubuntu. It includes six main editions, five immutable desktop variants, and 12 "spins" with different GUIs. The combined version 45 release notes detail some of the bigger individual component changes and note the hardware requirements. The recommended spec is now a 2 GHz quad-core CPU with 8 GB of RAM and 20 GB of disk space, and at least 1024×768 graphics. Fedora 45 supports most display adapters, but 3D acceleration may not work on older GPUs, including Intel models prior to GMA9xx, Nvidia models prior to NV30 (GeForce FX5xxx series), and AMD Radeon models prior to R300 (Radeon 9500). We took a quick look at the beta back in September, focusing on its new next-generation text console, which is a welcome change. We especially liked the ability to zoom in and out on the text console on the fly, which is something we've missed since the superb "Laptop Ultravision" for DOS , about a third of a century ago. (The company is long gone, but we found a downloadable version for all you DOS users .) The desktop flagship editions are Workstation 45 , which comes with GNOME 51 "A Coruña" , and Fedora KDE Plasma Desktop , with KDE Plasma 6.8 . We covered some of the new features in GNOME 51 when we looked at the Ubuntu 26.10 beta , and those changes apply here too – notably, improvements in the Settings app, but removal of some older Nvidia GPU support. Both the big names are Wayland-only environments now, but by our reckoning, X11 fans have seven of the 12 official spins to choose from: Xfce, Cinnamon, MATE, i3, LXQt, LXDE, and Sugar (SOAS) all still use X.org if you prefer. There is also a combined What's New page for all the Atomic Desktops, Fedora’s immutable variants – the main shared feature here being the new web-based installer. The new version of main Fedora is accompanied by Fedora Asahi Remix 45 for Apple Silicon Macs. This is a more notable release than the cross-platform editions, as Asahi 45 brings initial support for M3-based Macs as well as M1 and M2 kit. As The Reg described in September , though, the M3 support is preliminary and limited – for instance, it excludes the M3 Ultra. If you have an M3 Mac, for now, you're better off sticking to macOS. The most important changes in Fedora 45 are under the hood, which is what the Red Hat release announcement focuses on. It now uses RPM version 6.1, with enhanced package signature checking , and blocks the vendor of packages silently changing. The GNOME keyring now uses the oo7 secrets manager . Support for two old VPN plugins has been removed, because the packages were unmaintained. A feature that we are happy to see land at last is better support for Red Hat’s Stratis next-generation storage subsystem. We gave a potted overview of Stratis 3.3 back in 2022: it was on version 3.3 back then. It’s the same main Stratis version 3.9 we saw in Fedora 44, but the installation program now has support for installing Fedora 45 on Stratis storage . Stratis is Red Hat’s rival to OpenZFS. The plan is that Stratis offers similar features and resilience to ZFS, especially in the field of copy-on-write snapshots and simple multi-device logical volume management, but built from all-GPL code. Rather than a whole new filesystem, Stratis integrates XFS, LVM, and the kernel device-mapper functionality. Stratis 1.0 appeared in Fedora 29 eight years ago, and Fedora 45 has version 3.9.3. It's good to see it finally making real progress: if nothing else, we've seen Btrfs irretrievably corrupt a full volume far too many times to ever trust it again, so an alternative is very welcome. When we looked at Fedora 44 , we noted the difficulty of doing custom disk partitioning. It was there, but very well-hidden. Now, the installer can launch the Cockpit web-management tool to make it easier to set up your drives however you want. An interesting side-effect of the delayed release is that Fedora 45 ships with kernel 7.2 – specifically, version 7.2.15, which is the last release of this short-term series . In other words, it’s an end-of-life kernel version. It’s an amusing contrast to its near-contemporary Ubuntu 26.10, which shipped with a pre-release kernel . Our test Ubuntu box was automatically upgraded to the release version by the background automatic updates process , but to our surprise, it didn't receive the kernel update for over a week. This shouldn't be a problem: unlike Ubuntu, Fedora releases routinely receive updates to whole new kernel versions, so we’re sure Fedora 45 users will get kernel 7.3 very soon. We upgraded the same test machine on which we tried GNOME 48 in Fedora 42 early last year. You can skip one Fedora release on upgrade, but not two, so we had to go via Fedora 44 — which took some time, and threw up a minor packaging glitch, but it got there. The result runs surprisingly well, although this 2008 machine is well below the recommended spec. ®

item.title: Mohbad: DNA samples collected from son, remains
item.description: By Esther Onyegbula LAGOS — The paternity dispute surrounding Master Liam, son of late Nigerian singer Ilerioluwa Oladimeji Aloba, popularly known as Mohbad, has entered a new phase following the collection of DNA samples from the child and the singer’s remains under court supervision. The exercise took place on Saturday, October 31, 2026, following an application by Mohbad’s wife, Omowunmi Aloba, for a court-supervised DNA test to establish Liam’s paternity. The court granted the application and appointed a welfare officer to supervise the exercise, fixing October 31 for the collection of the samples. The paternity question had earlier been raised by Mohbad’s father, Mr Joseph Aloba, who also sought a DNA test to establish whether Liam was the deceased singer’s biological son. Proceedings relating to his request had, however, experienced delays. Security personnel were present during Saturday’s exercise to maintain order. Those in attendance included Mohbad’s mother, Mrs Abosede; his younger brother, Adura; and his wife, Omowunmi. The exercise reportedly became emotional during the identification of the late singer’s remains, which was part of the process. Samples were collected from Mohbad’s remains at Mainland General Hospital, popularly known as the Infectious Diseases Hospital (IDH), Yaba. The samples were subsequently taken to the Lagos State DNA and Forensic Centre, where Liam’s samples were also collected for forensic examination. Speaking after the exercise, the lawyer representing Omowunmi, Barrister Kabiru, said no date had been fixed for the release of the DNA results. He said the parties would be notified through the court once the results were available. Kabiru also commended the court and the Nigeria Police Force for their professionalism and support in ensuring that the exercise was completed. The DNA test is the latest development in the paternity dispute, which has attracted public attention since Mohbad’s death in September 2023. The results of the forensic examination are expected to provide scientific evidence to assist the court in resolving the paternity question. item.title: ‘Wellness is on the ballot’: why did so many pilates studios tell me to vote in the midterms?
item.description: Owners of pilates and yoga studios in the US got political and encouraged their followers to vote on social media Your local pilates instructors only want you to do two things: breathe through your side-planks and vote. In the days leading up to the US midterm elections, a wave of posts from fitness and wellness accounts blanketed Instagram, eschewing their typical messaging around the importance of strengthening your core in favor of the importance of exercising your civic duty. Owners of pilates and yoga studios and instructors across the US posted reels and pictures on platforms like Instagram encouraging their followers and clients to vote. Engagement varied depending on their following: posts reaped anywhere from 70 to more than 10,000 likes. Continue reading...

item.title: Tinubu’s aide highlights ‘technical glitches’ in US election
item.description: President Bola Tinubu’s aide, Tope Ajayi, has highlighted technical glitches and logistical problems that affected the American midterm election, drawing comparisons with criticism of Nigeria’s electoral process. Ajayi, Senior Special Assistant to the President on Media and Publicity, made the remarks in a post on X on Wednesday. He said despite reported problems with the election, political commentators and operatives in the United States had not discredited the process in the same way some Nigerians criticise elections in the country. “I have watched pundits and political operatives and partisan talking heads on various US television networks. Despite some of the technical glitches and logistical problems with the mid-term election they have not discredited the process like many of our people do here,” he wrote. I have watched pundits and political operatives and partisan talking heads on various US television networks. Despite some of the technical glitches and logistical problems with the mid-term election they have not discredited the process like many of our people do here. There… — Temitope Ajayi (@TheTope_Ajayi) November 4, 2026 Ajayi cited reports of ballot scanner programming glitches in parts of New York, equipment malfunction in Broward County, Florida, and ballot shortages in Kansas. He said the equipment malfunction in Broward County delayed the voting process, while a polling station in Kansas reportedly received only 100 paper ballots instead of 100,000. “There was also the case of 250,000 ballots that will be counted manually as a result technical problem with the voting machine,” Ajayi added. His comments come amid lingering controversy over the conduct of Nigeria’s 2023 presidential election, which was criticised by opposition parties and observers over technical and logistical problems. The post Tinubu’s aide highlights ‘technical glitches’ in US election appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Turn your home into a giant crane game with this open source robot
item.description: Your new robot servant doesn't have to look anything like a person or walk on two legs. In fact, it might just be a claw that hangs from the ceiling instead. That’s the future envisioned by Nathaniel Nifong, founder of Neufangled Robotics, and its Stringman robot . Put simply, Stringman is an AI-equipped claw suspended from four strings running through the corners of a room (up to 10 meters diagonally). Two motorized anchors adjust the lengths of the strings to move the claw around the room, from ceilings up to 4 meters high down to the floor to pick stuff up. With a payload capacity of around 2 kg, depending on its position, Stringman can move items to designated locations – like a toy box – and perform tidying tasks. Stringman can also be manually controlled if you’d prefer to play a room-sized crane game by yourself. According to Stringman’s documentation site, the device is currently a public prototype that “can self-calibrate in a new room and run policies, but is not yet reliable enough to be called a home appliance.” That said, demonstration videos on the website show it in action, and it’s neat to watch. Stringman is shown picking up laundry and dropping it in a basket, putting Lego bricks and other kids' toys back where they belong, and generally zooming around rooms and demonstrating its agility. One could imagine a properly trained Stringman could even grab the remote you left on the other side of the living room and drop it in your waiting hand if you’re that incredibly lazy. “Our mission is to give people an organized home,” Neufangled says on its future roadmap page . “We prioritize robots that are narrowly effective at something that helps today rather than a general purpose robot that may be in development for years.” The company further describes its goal as designing robots that are low cost and capable of doing things that people hate to do - e.g., pick up after a messy toddler - and making a robot that can do that while camouflaging itself into the home “as well as possible.” As long as you think a foot-long claw robot hanging from the corner of the ceiling is camouflaged, this is the robot for you. Neufangled lists Stringman for $795, which is a lot to ask for a public prototype that isn’t reliable enough to be called a home appliance yet. Luckily for those who’re interested in this sort of niche home automation, it’s fully open source , too. “A complete Stringman is three Raspberry Pis on your Wi-Fi network,” the documentation site reads: One in the gripper, and two in the corner anchor mounts that store line reels and have cameras to track the claw’s location as it moves around the room. A third camera mounted on the claw provides visual feedback. Oh, you'll also need a dedicated PC or Mac to run the robot's motion-control software. As for Stringman itself, to build your own, you'll need a 3D printer, a supplier to manufacture the PCBs, motors, Raspberry Pis, and other components listed in the bill of materials. You'll also
item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: Your new robot servant doesn't have to look anything like a person or walk on two legs. In fact, it might just be a claw that hangs from the ceiling instead. That’s the future envisioned by Nathaniel Nifong, founder of Neufangled Robotics, and its Stringman robot . Put simply, Stringman is an AI-equipped claw suspended from four strings running through the corners of a room (up to 10 meters diagonally). Two motorized anchors adjust the lengths of the strings to move the claw around the room, from ceilings up to 4 meters high down to the floor to pick stuff up. With a payload capacity of around 2 kg, depending on its position, Stringman can move items to designated locations – like a toy box – and perform tidying tasks. Stringman can also be manually controlled if you’d prefer to play a room-sized crane game by yourself. According to Stringman’s documentation site, the device is currently a public prototype that “can self-calibrate in a new room and run policies, but is not yet reliable enough to be called a home appliance.” That said, demonstration videos on the website show it in action, and it’s neat to watch. Stringman is shown picking up laundry and dropping it in a basket, putting Lego bricks and other kids' toys back where they belong, and generally zooming around rooms and demonstrating its agility. One could imagine a properly trained Stringman could even grab the remote you left on the other side of the living room and drop it in your waiting hand if you’re that incredibly lazy. “Our mission is to give people an organized home,” Neufangled says on its future roadmap page . “We prioritize robots that are narrowly effective at something that helps today rather than a general purpose robot that may be in development for years.” The company further describes its goal as designing robots that are low cost and capable of doing things that people hate to do - e.g., pick up after a messy toddler - and making a robot that can do that while camouflaging itself into the home “as well as possible.” As long as you think a foot-long claw robot hanging from the corner of the ceiling is camouflaged, this is the robot for you. Neufangled lists Stringman for $795, which is a lot to ask for a public prototype that isn’t reliable enough to be called a home appliance yet. Luckily for those who’re interested in this sort of niche home automation, it’s fully open source , too. “A complete Stringman is three Raspberry Pis on your Wi-Fi network,” the documentation site reads: One in the gripper, and two in the corner anchor mounts that store line reels and have cameras to track the claw’s location as it moves around the room. A third camera mounted on the claw provides visual feedback. Oh, you'll also need a dedicated PC or Mac to run the robot's motion-control software. As for Stringman itself, to build your own, you'll need a 3D printer, a supplier to manufacture the PCBs, motors, Raspberry Pis, and other components listed in the bill of materials. You'll also need to follow the guides on the documentation site to get it up and running, calibrate it for your space using printed markers, set up drop-off points using visual tags, and program it to perform tasks. But is it safe? One could imagine getting tangled in the lines if you get in Stringman’s way. Nifong admits that can happen, writing in the documentation that he has walked into the lines himself without injury. “I live with two of these, and I've walked into the lines before. It's startling, but harmless — they're light and they give,” he writes. According to the robot’s website, it has a tension limit of 28 newtons, or around six and a quarter pounds of force. If that limit is reached, all of the lines relax and can be pulled loose. Those who want to play with a simulated Stringman can do so on Stringman’s web portal , which includes options to connect to a personal machine over LAN, the cloud, or a simulated version. Hopefully it’s easier to work with than an arcade claw. ®

item.title: APC group insists Karimi won Kogi West senatorial primary
item.description: By Adeola Badru The Win With Tinubu (WWT) Grassroots Mobilisation Programme in Kogi State has insisted that Senator Sunday Steve Karimi remains the All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate for Kogi West Senatorial District in the 2027 general elections, despite a Federal High Court ruling nullifying his candidature. The group said the outcome of the May 18, 2026, APC senatorial primary was reviewed and upheld by the party’s appeal committee, following which Karimi’s name was submitted to and published by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) as the party’s candidate. It, however, disclosed that Karimi’s legal team had commenced steps to challenge the court ruling at the appellate court. The group’s position was contained in a statement issued on Wednesday by its State Programme Coordinator, Sani Philips, following the judgment delivered by Justice Salim Olasupo Ibrahim in a suit filed by Hon. Samuel Bamidele Aro against Karimi. The group argued that the court ruling should not override the outcome of the party’s internal electoral process, insisting that APC members and delegates in Kogi West had elected Karimi during the primary. It also recalled that controversy had trailed the primary after Aro’s name was allegedly submitted as the winner despite his purported non-participation in the exercise. According to WWT, the party’s appeal committee subsequently reviewed the process and reaffirmed Karimi’s victory. The statement said: “While we note with respect the ruling, we, however, consider it a needless distraction and a deliberate attempt to deny members of the APC in Kogi West the mandate freely given to Senator Sunday Steve Karimi through their votes at the APC Kogi West Senatorial Primaries Election, which took place on May 18, 2026.” The group further questioned aspects of the judgment, alleging that the trial judge departed from established legal principles in reaching his decision. It added that Karimi’s legal team had begun the process of filing an appeal to challenge and set aside the ruling. WWT maintained that Karimi remained the party’s duly nominated candidate pending the determination of the matter by the appellate court. It said: “We wish to affirm that Senator Sunday Steve Karimi remains the authentic, duly nominated and validly elected candidate of our great party for the Kogi West Senatorial District in the 2027 general elections, pending the determination of the suit at the appellate court.” Recounting the controversy surrounding the primary, the group alleged that Aro’s name had previously been submitted as the winner despite his not participating in the exercise. It said the APC appeal committee intervened, reviewed the process and upheld Karimi’s victory, after which his name was forwarded to INEC and published as the party’s candidate. The mobilisation group also disputed the court’s assessment of the primary, arguing that the ruling did not reflect the process conducted and documented by the relevant organs

It also recalled that controversy had trailed the primary after Aro’s name was allegedly submitted as the winner despite his purported non-participation in the exercise. The group, which disclosed that it was sponsored by Karimi, said its ward-level engagements and mobilisation activities would not be suspended because of the ongoing litigation. It described the senator as its chief grassroots mobiliser for Tinubu’s re-election campaign in Kogi State and reaffirmed its support for his bid to secure a second term in the Senate. The group expressed confidence that the appellate court would determine the matter expeditiously, while maintaining that the party’s political activities in Kogi West would continue. item.title: Nigeria’s Foreign Affairs minister appointed Commonwealth CMAG vice-chair
item.description: By Favour Ulebor, Abuja Nigeria’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu, has been appointed Vice-Chair of the Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG), giving the country a leadership role in the organisation’s efforts to uphold democracy, human rights and the rule of law. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced the appointment in a statement on Wednesday, saying it was made during the Group’s meeting on the sidelines of the ongoing 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM 2026) in St. John’s, Antigua and Barbuda. The meeting brought together leaders and representatives of the 56 Commonwealth member states, with King Charles III, Head of the Commonwealth, also in attendance. According to the ministry, Odumegwu-Ojukwu’s appointment places Nigeria in a strategic position to contribute to discussions and decisions on democratic governance, institutional accountability and the protection of fundamental rights across member countries. The Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group, chaired by Malta’s Chris Fearne, is a rotating body of foreign ministers mandated to uphold the organisation’s fundamental political values, including democracy, human rights, good governance and the rule of law. Established in 1995 under the Millbrook Commonwealth Action Plan, CMAG serves as a mechanism for responding to serious or persistent violations of these shared values by member states. Its responsibilities include assessing political developments in member countries and recommending appropriate collective action where necessary. The group initially focused largely on unconstitutional changes of government, particularly military coups. However, its mandate was expanded by Commonwealth leaders in 2011 to allow more proactive engagement with countries facing threats to democratic governance. Its areas of concern now include unconstitutional changes to political arrangements, suspension of parliaments, electoral irregularities, restrictions on political participation, interference with judicial independence, human rights violations and restrictions on the media and civil society. The ministry said the appointment underscored Nigeria’s continued engagement with the Commonwealth and its commitment to promoting dialogue, cooperation and respect for the shared principles of the 56-member organisation. The post Nigeria’s Foreign Affairs minister appointed Commonwealth CMAG vice-chair appeared first on Vanguard News .

According to the ministry, Odumegwu-Ojukwu’s appointment places Nigeria in a strategic position to contribute to discussions and decisions on democratic governance, institutional accountability and the protection of fundamental rights across member countries. The Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group, chaired by Malta’s Chris Fearne, is a rotating body of foreign ministers mandated to uphold the organisation’s fundamental political values, including democracy, human rights, good governance and the rule of law. Established in 1995 under the Millbrook Commonwealth Action Plan, CMAG serves as a mechanism for responding to serious or persistent violations of these shared values by member states. Its responsibilities include assessing political developments in member countries and recommending appropriate collective action where necessary. The group initially focused largely on unconstitutional changes of government, particularly military coups. However, its mandate was expanded by Commonwealth leaders in 2011 to allow more proactive engagement with countries facing threats to democratic governance. Its areas of concern now include unconstitutional changes to political arrangements, suspension of parliaments, electoral irregularities, restrictions on political participation, interference with judicial independence, human rights violations and restrictions on the media and civil society. The ministry said the appointment underscored Nigeria’s continued engagement with the Commonwealth and its commitment to promoting dialogue, cooperation and respect for the shared principles of the 56-member organisation. item.title: Namibia President declares Dangote’s $2.5bn energy investment a landmark for Africa’s industrial future
item.description: …Says project launch most memorable day of her presidency …Unveils 600-million-litre tank farm, 1,700km regional pipeline By Udeme Akpan President of Namibia, Dr Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, has described the $2.5 billion Dangote Namibia Tank Farm and Regional Pipeline Project as a landmark investment that will accelerate Africa’s industrialisation, enhance regional energy security and deepen economic integration across Southern Africa. Speaking at the project’s official launch in Walvis Bay, the Namibian leader praised Aliko Dangote, President and Chief Executive of Dangote Industries Limited, for demonstrating confidence in Africa’s economic potential through transformative investments in energy infrastructure. She described the occasion as the most memorable day of her presidency. “Today, is the most memorable day of my presidency,” she said, noting that the investment reflects the growing capacity of African entrepreneurs to drive the continent’s transformation. The project comprises a proposed 600-million-litre petroleum storage facility and an approximately 1,700-kilometre regional pipeline network that will position Namibia as a strategic fuel distribution hub for Southern Africa. The infrastructure is expected to improve fuel supply reliability, reduce transportation costs and support economic growth across the region. President Nandi-Ndaitwah said the investment aligns with Namibia’s development priorities and the goals of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), while creating opportunities for employment, skills transfer and industrial expansion. Addressing the ceremony, Aliko Dangote said the investment forms part of the Group’s broader vision to build interconnected centres of production, storage and distribution across Africa. He disclosed that the facility, located near Walvis Bay, will have storage capacity for 360 million litres of diesel and 240 million litres of petrol. The pipeline network will connect Namibia to key markets in Botswana, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Malawi and parts of the Democratic Republic of Congo. “We want to invest heavily so that landlocked countries can access petroleum products at cheaper prices,” Dangote said. Dangote also announced that the Group has increased its Africa-wide investment ambition towards 2030 from $50 billion to $60 billion, signalling plans for further expansion across the continent. “What we are launching today represents an investment of $2.5 billion, but Namibia deserves much more. We want to invest more and do more with your government,” he said. Reaffirming his commitment to Africa’s development, Dangote said the continent possesses the resources, talent and markets needed to achieve sustainable industrialisation. “Africa must industrialise Africa,” he declared. The Governor of Namibia’s Erongo Region, Dr Nathalia ǀGoagoses, also welcomed the investment, describing it as a strategic initiative that will strengthen Namibia’s role as a gateway for trade, investment and regional economic

item.title: Enugu Air secures approval for Lagos–London route
item.description: By Dickson Omobola Enugu State-owned airline, Enugu Air, has secured approval to operate the Lagos–London Gatwick route, with Omni-Blu Aviation appointed as the designated operator under a strategic partnership. The airline said the approval marked a significant step in its expansion plans, with the proposed route expected to strengthen air connectivity between Nigeria and the United Kingdom and create new opportunities for passenger travel and trade. It added that the development aligned with the aviation vision of Enugu State Governor, Dr Peter Mbah, to position the state as an emerging hub for international connectivity, investment, tourism and economic growth. item.title: Boffins use machine-learning tricks to create a starlight dimmer switch
item.description: Scientists have developed a way to remove starlight from telescope images that improved sensitivity to faint exoplanets by up to 15 times in tests on James Webb Space Telescope data. A team led by Northwestern University's Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez combined a physics-based telescope model with optimization techniques used in machine learning to subtract unwanted starlight. Directly imaging exoplanets remains difficult because their host stars' glare can overwhelm their faint light. Existing techniques subtract modeled or reference starlight, but tiny changes in telescope optics can leave residual glare that hides planets. The team's Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP) framework models how light passes through the telescope, adjusts for optical imperfections, and simulates the glare to be subtracted. Applied to observations from Webb's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam), FLIP produced the first image of the known giant planet 51 Eridani b at an infrared wavelength of 4.3 micrometers, where conventional processing had failed. Tests showed sensitivity improvements of two to 15 times over conventional techniques, according to the Nature paper . "This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories… potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success," the paper says. Further work includes reducing computational demands and developing ways to handle the much larger data volumes produced by ground-based observations. The researchers hope further development and testing will bring direct images of Earth-like planets closer, while reducing the extent to which tiny telescope instabilities obscure them. ®

item.title: Democrats warn Trump camp to ‘lawyer up’ as anger over corruption drives midterms wipeout
item.description: Corruption in government was high on the minds of US voters as they dealt US President Donald Trump’s party a chastening defeat in midterm elections, toppling Republican strongholds like dominoes and flipping both chambers of Congress. Triumphant Democrats have warned the Trump administration to “lawyer up”; how they go about tackling alleged graft and abuse of power could shape both their own fortunes and the country’s politics.

item.title: People say they want small smartphones—the Enough Phone will put that to the test
item.description: The first modern smartphones had 3.5-inch screens, which can be hard to remember in today's world of gargantuan glass slabs. Sure, people talk about wanting smaller phones, but will they buy one? Enough Phone is betting they will. The company will begin taking preorders for its first device today, which is built around a petite 5.3-inch screen that is apparently the smallest it could find with decent performance metrics. The company's cheeky name is reflected in its approach to phone design. A flagship killer this is not, but it's probably "enough" for most people. It has a mid-range MediaTek processor, a single rear-facing camera, a polycarbonate body, and a fingerprint sensor in the power button. Specs at a glance: Enough Phone ($399 for a limited time, $599 MSRP) SoC MediaTek Dimensity 7500 Memory 8GB Storage 128GB with microSD Display 5.3-inch 1520x720 HD+ LCD Cameras Sony IMX766 50 MP, 32 MP selfie Software Android 17 or OdysseyOS Battery 3500 mAh (removable) Connectivity 5G, LTE, Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth, NFC, SIM+eSIM Measurements 133×64×12 mm With that compact screen, the Enough Phone will be dwarfed by almost every existing smartphone. While it's a bit thicker, the device has almost the same footprint as the iPhone 13 Mini. Thinness takes a hit, as the designers have opted to make the battery user-replaceable. Like the Fairphone , you'll just have to remove a few screws to get the back cover off. Read full article Comments

item.title: NASA Announces Ka-Band Satellite Relay Awards for Space Communications
item.description: Credit: NASA NASA selected three companies on Wednesday to perform work to develop Ka-band space relay capability concepts that are compatible with current missions in space, ensuring service continuity for existing spacecraft without requiring modifications to their onboard systems. Through this work, NASA will aim to acquire end-to-end solutions that include space, ground, launch, operations, and integration elements, as one of many customers in the commercial marketplace. The awards, under the Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships-3 Broad Agency Announcement Appendix E, are firm-fixed-price contracts that give NASA the option to provide additional funding up to the award limit to advance from initial concept development and risk reduction to an in-orbit flight demonstration. The initial period of performance runs from Nov. 4 through May 3, 2027, with additional priced options to continue work through 2029. The contract awardees with maximum potential value inclusive of all future options are: Astranis Space Technologies Corp. for $264.3 million. Global Enterprise Solutions Inc. for $340.4 million. Viasat Inc. for $460.9 million. Facilitated through the agency’s SCaN (Space Communications and Navigation) program’s Communications Services Project, this work supports NASA’s decision to gradually retire the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet and adopt commercial services for future missions. In addition to the commercial capabilities currently under development by the program’s industry partners, Ka-band services are needed to support select in-orbit missions that cannot feasibly modify flight hardware or transition to non-compatible commercial services. To learn more about NASA’s Network Extension for User Continuity and Sustainability Ka-band service acquisition, visit: https://go.nasa.gov/4iVfeVB -end- Jennifer Dooren / Jessica Taveau Headquarters, Washington 202-358-1600 jennifer.m.dooren@nasa.gov / jessica.c.taveau@nasa.gov Share Details Last Updated Nov 04, 2026 Editor Jessica Taveau Location NASA Headquarters Related Terms Space Communications & Navigation Program Space Communications Technology

item.title: A dyslexia diagnosis can help struggling children, but what about the rest?
item.description: Shutterstock/Jakub Krechowicz In years gone by, children who struggled to learn to read and spell were labelled “stupid”, “lazy” or “dim”. Today, of course, we are much more enlightened – now we label many of these children as “dyslexic”. But perhaps this label is still a bad idea. Picture two 9-year-olds reading at the level of an average 6-year-old. One gets a diagnosis of dyslexia. This positively affects her wellbeing. Her teachers now understand she has dyslexia and that she can get tailored help. The other child isn’t so lucky. Maybe his parents can’t afford a dyslexia test – in the UK, assessment isn’t available on the NHS and can cost several hundred pounds. In the US it could set parents back thousands of dollars. Or perhaps he was tested but the result was negative. Until very recently, this outcome was common for already disadvantaged children, because the official definition of dyslexia included the idea of “discrepancy” – that reading problems should be unexpected given a child’s other cognitive abilities. Assessing ability using IQ tests can also be biased against those from lower socioeconomic groups or learning to read in a second language. By extension, this second child is just bad at reading or lazy, or both, and not eligible to receive extra help with reading. Advertisement Two children with the same learning difficulty. One gets help, the other does not Two children with the same learning difficulty. One gets help and understanding and the other doesn’t, all because of a label. Yet this label is based on a questionable assessment. Despite trials using a wide range of cognitive processes, researchers have been unable to find meaningful ways to identify dyslexia. So, why not just help all children who struggle to read? Each has a unique combination of risk and remediation factors, but all will benefit most if we intervene when the problem first shows up, instead of waiting years for them to fail and then receive a diagnosis. Our newfound understanding of what is happening in their brains even suggests some surprisingly simple ways to help . Giving every child the best possible chance to overcome their challenge is what matters, not the label we attach to them.

item.title: The DNA is backwards on The Selfish Gene’s cover – again
item.description: Josie Ford Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more Don’t get it twisted Feedback is not young. We have been here on the back pages for many years, endlessly pushing a boulder up a hill and trying to take joy in the effort. This means, every so often, we are forced to repeat ourselves – because the world repeats itself. With a due sense of ennui, we turn our world-weary eyes to the cover of the new 50th anniversary edition of Richard Dawkins’s popular science classic The Selfish Gene . The title, written in all-caps, takes up most of the cover. The “I” in “SELFISH” has been replaced by a colourful little drawing of a DNA double helix. Advertisement Alas, something is awry. Geneticist Simon Fisher pointed it out on Bluesky : “You know a gene is selfish when its DNA twists the wrong way, as demonstrated by the left-handed double-helix proudly adorning the 50th Anniversary Edition of the multimillion copy bestseller on this topic.” Yes, once again we have an example of a DNA molecule being drawn, essentially, backwards. In reality, it is a right-handed double helix, but the one on the book cover is left-handed. It’s twisting the wrong way. Feedback’s mind’s eye immediately cast itself back to March 2025 , when we covered a Lego model that included many scientific and technological objects, including a sadly left-handed DNA. It turns out that The Selfish Gene ‘s art has been wrong for at least a decade. Patrick Goymer , an editor at PLOS One , shared the cover of the 40th anniversary edition on Bluesky, and it has the same left-handed DNA in place of the “I”. Feedback notes that our own copy is the 30th anniversary edition, and the DNA is correct. At some point since 2006, the DNA on the cover has flipped into a mirror universe. This little mistake would be doubly embarrassing if, say, the Nobel prize in chemistry had recently been awarded for research into these sorts of mirror molecules. Can you imagine? Coca-Cola faecaloma Sometimes a scientific paper has a title so vivid, so immediate, that Feedback just has to write about it. Such is the case with a paper published in Cureus , titled: “Massive fecaloma dissolved by Coca-Cola: A case report”. It was sent to us by Australia reporter Alice Klein, who either has a truly terrible browser history or makes extensive use of a VPN. A faecaloma, for those not yet blessed with the knowledge, is a large lump of impacted faeces trapped in a person’s rectum. In this case report, the faecaloma had a maximum diameter of 12.2 centimetres. Readers anxious to see a dramatisation of such a condition are advised to try series two , episode five of The Pitt , in which one of the patients has impacted faeces that the doctors must manually dislodge. Based on our own personal experience, we do not recommend watching this sequence over dinner. With a due sense of ennui, we turn our world-weary eyes to the cover of the new 50th anniversary edition of Richard Dawkins’s popular science classic The Selfish Gene . The title, written in all-caps, takes up most of the cover. The “I” in “SELFISH” has been replaced by a colourful little drawing of a DNA double helix. Advertisement Alas, something is awry. Geneticist Simon Fisher pointed it out on Bluesky : “You know a gene is selfish when its DNA twists the wrong way, as demonstrated by the left-handed double-helix proudly adorning the 50th Anniversary Edition of the multimillion copy bestseller on this topic.” Yes, once again we have an example of a DNA molecule being drawn, essentially, backwards. In reality, it is a right-handed double helix, but the one on the book cover is left-handed. It’s twisting the wrong way. Feedback’s mind’s eye immediately cast itself back to March 2025 , when we covered a Lego model that included many scientific and technological objects, including a sadly left-handed DNA. It turns out that The Selfish Gene ‘s art has been wrong for at least a decade. Patrick Goymer , an editor at PLOS One , shared the cover of the 40th anniversary edition on Bluesky, and it has the same left-handed DNA in place of the “I”. Feedback notes that our own copy is the 30th anniversary edition, and the DNA is correct. At some point since 2006, the DNA on the cover has flipped into a mirror universe. This little mistake would be doubly embarrassing if, say, the Nobel prize in chemistry had recently been awarded for research into these sorts of mirror molecules. Can you imagine? Coca-Cola faecaloma Sometimes a scientific paper has a title so vivid, so immediate, that Feedback just has to write about it. Such is the case with a paper published in Cureus , titled: “Massive fecaloma dissolved by Coca-Cola: A case report”. It was sent to us by Australia reporter Alice Klein, who either has a truly terrible browser history or makes extensive use of a VPN. A faecaloma, for those not yet blessed with the knowledge, is a large lump of impacted faeces trapped in a person’s rectum. In this case report, the faecaloma had a maximum diameter of 12.2 centimetres. Readers anxious to see a dramatisation of such a condition are advised to try series two , episode five of The Pitt , in which one of the patients has impacted faeces that the doctors must manually dislodge. Based on our own personal experience, we do not recommend watching this sequence over dinner. Back in the real world, the doctors reported that they tried “conservative management”, which apparently consisted of “polyethylene glycol, senna, mineral oil, and sodium phosphate enemas”. But the faecaloma didn’t budge, so they turned to a more drastic solution. The authors tell us that “isolated case reports have described the use of Coca-Cola enemas for fecaloma dissolution with favorable outcomes”. This is because “Classic Coca-Cola acts as a mucolytic agent [it makes mucus less thick and sticky], a source of carbonic acid, and an effervescent solvent”. Hence the doctors administered two 1-litre Coca-Cola enemas, which shrank the faecaloma enough to resolve the situation. Feedback has a number of thoughts, such as: would Pepsi work as well? What if the doctors had first inserted Mentos? We are also not sure we ever want to put Coca-Cola into our mouth ever again: if it can be used to destroy a faecaloma, we dread to think what it might be doing to our teeth. @2, Brute? Some weeks ago, Feedback began investigating unfortunate technology-induced truncations and abbreviations. These truncations have gone on for a long time and there is no end in sight. Stuart Arnold was bemused to find Facebook recommending a post about an obsolete form of aircraft called a Rotodyne, which never made it past the prototype phase. It is best described as “a plane, but stick a set of helicopter rotors on top”. Unfortunately, due to the character limit in the Facebook feed, the post was cut off as follows: “designed to take off vertically, then fly faster and fart…” “It’s probably a good thing that the program was cancelled,” says Stuart. Secondly, David Smith encountered a related problem: tech-induced rudeness. Because his name is a common one, he has long struggled to find unique identifiers for email addresses and such. Imagine his surprise when he joined a large organisation and found he was only the second person there with that name. This seemed like (minor) good news, but he swiftly discovered a downside to being the second David Smith. “The part of the email address corresponding to ‘2@’ has to be pronounced very carefully,” he says. And finally, Andy Howe reminds us that Trinity Hall, one of the Cambridge colleges, “is colloquially abbreviated as Tit”. He tells us: “This was particularly unfortunate for an archaeology student who saw his name listed in a society’s membership records, followed by the descriptor ‘Arch Tit’.” Got a story for Feedback? You can send stories to Feedback by email at feedback@newscientist.com . Please include your home address. This week’s and past Feedbacks can be seen on our website .

item.title: 2027: We won’t endorse any candidate — Health workers
item.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ABUJA — Ahead of the 2027 elections, the Medical and Health Workers Union of Nigeria (MHWUN) on Wednesday declared that its members will not endorse or finance any candidate. The health workers also said they are rejecting a spectator role in the forthcoming elections and demanded binding commitments on CONHESS and outstanding arrears. Speaking in his welcome address at the 52nd session of the National Executive Council (NEC) meeting in Abuja, the President of the Medical and Health Workers Union of Nigeria, Comrade Kabiru Ado Sani, said the union will enter the 2027 general election neither as party loyalists nor as passive observers, but as an organised constituency demanding enforceable commitments on welfare, CONHESS arrears, and outstanding collective agreements. In a strongly worded position ahead of the polls, the union said the question confronting health workers is no longer whether they will participate in the election, but on what terms. “The permutation is now upon us. The question is no longer whether health workers will be in it, but whether we shall be in it as spectators, as foot soldiers, or as a constituency with a strong position,” the MHWUN President said. He warned that health workers must not allow their numerical strength and professional importance to be reduced to election-season mobilisation for politicians who may abandon their concerns afterwards. MHWUN insisted that it remains a trade union, not a political party, and would not endorse any candidate or political platform. “MHWUN is a trade union, not a political party. We will not endorse any party or candidate, and the funds of this Union will not be used to finance any of them,” the union leader stated. item.dc:creator: Nwafor
item.content:encoded: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ABUJA — Ahead of the 2027 elections, the Medical and Health Workers Union of Nigeria (MHWUN) on Wednesday declared that its members will not endorse or finance any candidate. The health workers also said they are rejecting a spectator role in the forthcoming elections and demanded binding commitments on CONHESS and outstanding arrears. Speaking in his welcome address at the 52nd session of the National Executive Council (NEC) meeting in Abuja, the President of the Medical and Health Workers Union of Nigeria, Comrade Kabiru Ado Sani, said the union will enter the 2027 general election neither as party loyalists nor as passive observers, but as an organised constituency demanding enforceable commitments on welfare, CONHESS arrears, and outstanding collective agreements. In a strongly worded position ahead of the polls, the union said the question confronting health workers is no longer whether they will participate in the election, but on what terms. “The permutation is now upon us. The question is no longer whether health workers will be in it, but whether we shall be in it as spectators, as foot soldiers, or as a constituency with a strong position,” the MHWUN President said. He warned that health workers must not allow their numerical strength and professional importance to be reduced to election-season mobilisation for politicians who may abandon their concerns afterwards. MHWUN insisted that it remains a trade union, not a political party, and would not endorse any candidate or political platform. “MHWUN is a trade union, not a political party. We will not endorse any party or candidate, and the funds of this Union will not be used to finance any of them,” the union leader stated. He added that members remain free to vote according to their conscience, stressing that no individual has the authority to speak for the union while campaigning for a party. “Our members are free to vote their conscience, and no one speaks for this Union when speaking for a party,” he said. The union argued that its political influence should not depend on telling members whom to vote for, but on forcing every contender for power to confront the health sector’s unresolved demands. “Our influence does not lie in telling members how to vote. It lies in making the health worker’s agenda impossible to ignore, whoever wins,” the MHWUN political head declared. He explained that at the centre of that agenda are the CONHESS salary structure, unpaid arrears, and collective agreements reached with the Federal Government but yet to be fully implemented. The union framed its demands in legal as well as moral terms, insisting that agreements signed by the Federal Government cannot be treated as disposable political promises. “A collective agreement signed by the Federal Government is an obligation of the State,” Dr. Sani said. “It does not lapse when a tenure ends, and no incoming administration is entitled to treat it as the debt of its predecessor.” He warned that any administration emerging from the 2027 polls would inherit not only government assets and the treasury, but also outstanding obligations to health workers. “Whoever is declared winner after 16th January will inherit the CONHESS table, the arrears, and the unconcluded negotiations, along with the Treasury,” he said. While pressing for a strong health-worker voice, MHWUN urged members to participate lawfully and peacefully in the electoral process, avoiding conduct capable of damaging the union’s reputation or exposing members to risk. “I therefore urge every member to take part peacefully in the electoral process and not to take any action that would smear the good name of the union or jeopardise the interest of our members,” the union leader said. He described the session as taking place at “a defining moment in our nation’s history,” citing a challenging economy and a general election just weeks away. “Comrades, specifically, in less than eleven weeks, Nigerians will go to the polls. Between now and then, every candidate of every party will discover and acknowledge health workers.” He warned that health workers would be courted with familiar political language. “We will be called heroes, pillars of the nation, and the conscience of the health system. We shall hear it all with courtesy sugar-coated in a political tongue. But let us remember that warm words cost nothing, and that they have never paid a salary, cleared an arrear, or built infrastructure.” The 52nd NEC meeting is holding under the theme, “Health Workers and Socio-Economic Crisis: Implications for the 2027 General Election.” According to the MHWUN President, the theme is “not an invitation to join the political contest as a worker,” but “a clarion call to health workers to understand the implications of the outcome of the 2027 general election and how it affects the social and economic conditions of the Nigerian health worker.” He said the Joint Health Sector Unions (JOHESU) has remained a potent instrument in the struggle for better welfare for health workers and improved funding of the health sector. “CONHESS adjustment is one demand that is central to JOHESU’s struggle in the last thirteen years. This demand has led to many strike actions, the last being the historic 84-day strike action, which was suspended on 5th February 2026 on the strength of a signed Terms of Settlement (ToS) with the Federal Government. “Regrettably, the Federal Government seems not to have learnt any lesson from the last strike action, as it has continued to drag and delay the matter against the spirit of the Terms of Settlement. “The April 2026 date that was promised for implementation has passed without the CONHESS. “Meanwhile, we are waiting for further directives from the two Labour Centres, the NLC and TUC, who promised to take over the demands,” he concluded. The post 2027: We won’t endorse any candidate — Health workers appeared first on Vanguard News .
